# Effectiveness of a Fourth Dose of COVID-19 mRNA Vaccine in Patients with Systemic Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases Using Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs: An Emulated Target Trial

**Authors:** Jennifer S. Hanberg; Xiaoqing Fu; Xiaosong Wang; Naomi J. Patel; Yumeko Kawano; Abigail Schiff; Emily N. Kowalski; Claire E. Cook; Kathleen M.M. Vanni; Krishan Guzzo; Grace Qian; Katarina J. Bade; Alene Saavedra; Rathnam Venkat; Shruthi Srivatsan; Yuqing Zhang; Jeffrey A. Sparks; Zachary S. Wallace

**Affiliations:** 1Division of Rheumatology, Inflammation, and Immunity, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 2Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 3Division of Rheumatology, Allergy, and Immunology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 4Rheumatology and Allergy Clinical Epidemiology Research Center, Mongan Institute, Department of Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

Patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs) using disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) may have blunted responses to COVID-19 vaccines. The initial mRNA vaccine series is defined as 3 doses for this population and a 4th dose, or “booster,” is recommended. The effectiveness of the 4th dose in patients with SARDs using DMARDs is not well established.

We conducted an emulated target trial using observational data from the Mass General Brigham healthcare system to compare receiving vs. not yet receiving a 4th mRNA vaccine dose. Analyzed patients had SARDs, were prescribed DMARDs, and were eligible for a 4th dose of BNT162b2 or mRNA-1273 between 16/Jan/2022–11/Jun/2022. To account for temporal changes, the study period was divided into 1-week intervals. 4th-dose-exposed patients were included in a 1-week interval if they received a 4th mRNA dose in that interval; 4th-dose-unexposed were eligible for but had not yet received the 4th dose. The primary outcome was SARS-CoV-2 infection; the secondary outcome was severe SARS-CoV-2 infection (i.e., hospitalization/death). We assessed the effectiveness of the 4th dose using time-stratified, overlap propensity score-weighted Cox regression models.

We included 4305 patients, 3126 of whom received a 4th dose. Approximately half (54%, 1392/2563 after overlap weighting in both groups) had rheumatoid arthritis; the most frequent treatments were conventional synthetic DMARDs (58%, 1489/2563) or biologic DMARDs (39%, 1005/2563). SARS-CoV-2 infection risk was lower among patients receiving vs. not yet receiving a 4th dose (HR 0·59; 95%CI: 0·47, 0·74). A 4th dose reduced the risk of hospitalization or death within 14 days of SARS-CoV-2 infection (HR 0·35; 95% CI: 0·14, 0·85).

In this emulated target trial, a 4th dose of mRNA vaccine reduced COVID-19 risk by 41% and severe COVID-19 by 65% among SARD patients using DMARDs during the Omicron era. Patients with SARDs should be encouraged to remain up to date with COVID-19 vaccinations.

## Introduction

Many patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs) receiving disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) are at an increased risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection, including death due to COVID-19, compared to immunocompetent patients.1 In addition to the use of DMARDs, comorbidity burdens, SARD activity, and dysregulated immune responses also contribute to this risk.1–3 However, many patients with SARDs receiving DMARD therapy also have blunted humoral responses to COVID-19 vaccines, which remain the most important tool for preventing SARS-CoV-2 infection, especially severe disease, even against SARS-CoV-2 variants.4–8 Although there is inter-individual variation in vaccine immunogenicity,9 this phenomenon has been observed across multiple immunomodulatory therapy types, including conventional synthetic, targeted synthetic, and biologic DMARDs. Due to the blunted vaccine response in patients receiving DMARDs, the initial mRNA vaccine series was revised to include 3 doses for this population by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).10

A 4th (or first “booster”, for patients receiving a 3-dose “primary” series) dose was first recommended by the CDC in October 2021.11 This recommendation arrived among substantial evidence that vaccine effectiveness wanes over time, both with respect to prevention of any symptomatic disease and prevention of severe disease; such findings have been reported in patients with and without SARDs.12,13,7

In the general population, a 4th vaccine dose reduces the risk of breakthrough infection.14 Further, several studies have established that a 4th dose of mRNA vaccine improves the humoral response in many patients with SARDs using DMARDs.15–18 However, uptake of a 4th dose among patients with immunocompromising conditions, including DMARD users, has been slow.19 Additionally, the clinical effectiveness of the 4th dose in this population has not been well established. The current body of evidence includes a large study from a national healthcare system that found a protective effect; however, this study was not restricted to patients receiving DMARDs, excluded those with prior history of COVID-19 infection, was unable to confirm SARD diagnosis by chart review and included only patients receiving mRNA vaccine BNT162b2.20 Additional data on the effectiveness of a 4th mRNA vaccine dose may be helpful for informing patient decision making.

We aimed to assess the effectiveness of receiving vs not yet receiving a 4th dose of COVID-19 mRNA vaccine using a target trial framework, in a cohort of SARD patients receiving DMARD therapy that controlled for temporal trends.

## Methods

### Study Design and Population

We conducted an emulated target trial to compare the intervention of receiving (“exposed”) vs. not yet receiving a 4th vaccine (“unexposed”) among patients with SARDs using DMARDs in a cohort study using data from the Mass General Brigham (MGB) healthcare system.21,22 The full specification of the target trial is detailed in Tables S1 and S2.

MGB is a multi-center healthcare system that includes a total of 14 hospitals as well as primary care and specialty outpatient centers in the greater Boston, Massachusetts area. We limited our study population to Massachusetts residents (as obtained by primary address in the electronic health record [EHR]) because vaccination data from the Massachusetts state database was populated in the EHR and all immunizations administered in Massachusetts are required by law to be reported to the Massachusetts Immunization Information System.23

### Identification of Patients with SARDs

We included patients who had SARDs, as identified by a validated, rules-based algorithm including International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes and DMARD use; details of cohort assembly have previously been published.24 25 The assembly of the cohort from the EHR is depicted in Figure S1 and the list of ICD codes is provided in Table S3. The patient’s primary SARD diagnosis was based on ICD-10 codes, as previously described. We manually reviewed a subset of 50 cases in this cohort and found a positive predictive value (PPV) of 90% for identification of SARDs.25 Cases with ICD codes associated with diseases that can coexist (e.g., seronegative spondyloarthopathy and giant cell arteritis) or can exist as overlap disease (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis) were categorized as “multiple” primary rheumatic diseases. Medication data documented or prescribed in the EHR, was extracted as structured data within 12 months prior to the 3rd mRNA vaccine dose.25 Medications were categorized as conventional synthetic DMARD (csDMARD), biologic DMARD (bDMARD; excluding rituximab), rituximab, targeted synthetic DMARD (tsDMARD), or oral glucocorticoids.

From this population of patients with SARDs using DMARDs, we included patients who were eligible (by CDC guidelines) to receive a 4th dose of BNT162b2 or mRNA-1273 between 16/Jan/2022–11/Jun/2022, and therefore had received at least 3 doses of mRNA vaccine with the last dose occurring no later than 14/Mar/22. The primary circulating SARS-CoV-2 variant in Massachusetts during the study period was the omicron variant (lineages 21K, 21L, and 22C).26,27 We excluded recipients of Ad26.COV2.S. Although the initial recommendation for a 4th dose in this group was made in October 2021, we analyzed patients who were eligible to receive their 4th dose starting on 16/Jan/22 because there were too few patients who were eligible (based on the timing of their 3rd dose) prior to this. Patients with a history of SARS-CoV-2 infection prior to the study period were eligible for inclusion. Full inclusion and exclusion criteria are detailed in Table S1.

### Identification of the 4th-dose-exposed and 4th-dose-unexposed groups

To account for temporal changes in COVID-19 variants and guidance on 4th dose eligibility, the study period was divided into 1-week intervals for time-stratified analysis. The exposed cohort for each 1-week interval included those who received a 4th mRNA vaccine dose in that interval; unexposed participants were eligible for a 4th dose during the same interval but had not yet received it before or during the interval. Thus, an individual patient could be included multiple times as an unexposed participant but only once in the exposed cohort. The index date or “time zero” was defined as follows: in the exposed cohort, the index date was the date of 4th dose; for unexposed participants, it was a random date within the 1-week interval in question. Additionally, unexposed participants were required to have an inter-dose duration (the time from 3rd dose to index date) no less than the minimum and no greater than the maximum of the inter-dose duration among the exposed cohort for each interval, to account for possible waning of vaccine effect over time and ensure that the inter-dose interval was comparable between the exposed and unexposed cohorts. We did not specify a delay from vaccination to beginning of follow-up because the interval between vaccination and immune effect has not been clearly established in this population; not including a delay provides a conservative estimate of the efficacy of the 4th dose. The process by which the exposed and unexposed groups were assembled, and Time Zero determined, is further detailed in Figure S2.

### Outcome Ascertainment

The primary outcome was SARS-CoV-2 infection, defined by (1) positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR, (2) patient report of positive antigen test to the hospital/clinic, or (3) a positive COVID-19 “flag” (annotation by providers that a positive COVID test was reported) in the EHR, similar to the definition used in our prior work.24,25,28 Outcomes were analyzed in a per-protocol fashion. We did not require a record of symptomatic infection. The prespecified secondary outcome was hospitalization or death within 14 days of SARS-CoV-2 infection.

### Covariates

Data regarding demographics and comorbidities were extracted using electronic query, as previously described.25 Baseline characteristics including demographics (including age, sex, race and ethnicity as obtained from the EHR), comorbidities including interstitial lung disease as well as all components of the Charlson Comorbidity Index as defined by ICD-10 codes, smoking history, and body mass index (BMI) were assessed in the one year prior to the 3rd dose of vaccine. Prior SARS-CoV-2 infection was assessed in each time interval as a time-varying covariate, using the definition detailed under Outcome Ascertainment. Area-level income was assessed using ZIP code-based data from the US Census Bureau. We calculated the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) using all available data from comorbidities as ascertained by ICD-10 in the one year prior to the 3rd dose of vaccine. 29

### Statistical Analysis

Descriptive statistics were reported as mean +/− standard deviation, median (interquartile range) or frequency with proportion. In each 1-week time block, we calculated a propensity score (PS) using logistic regression models.30,31 We selected covariates for propensity score calculation a priori based on clinical experience and hypothesized causal pathways as detailed in the directed acyclic graph (Figure S3). The propensity score (PS) for receiving the 4th dose was calculated for participants in each weekly interval using a logistic regression, which included age, sex, race, ethnicity, BMI, smoking, median area-level income, Charlson Comorbidity Index, interstitial lung disease, type of rheumatic disease, type of DMARD, history of prior COVID-19 infection, and type of primary mRNA vaccine series. We applied overlap weighting of the PS to balance baseline characteristics between the comparison groups; the target population of overlap weighting emphasizes patients with the most overlap in their observed characteristic, and its corresponding estimand is the average treatment effect in the overlap population. 30,31 We assessed the distribution of baseline characteristics between two comparison cohorts before and after overlap weighting using the absolute standardized differences, with a cutpoint of 0.1 for assessment of balance. The absolute number of participants in each group and subgroup after overlap weighting is estimated based on the assigned weights.

Participants were followed from the index date (the determination of which is detailed in Figure S2) until the earliest of (1) outcome of interest; (2) bivalent vaccine availability (1 Sep 2022); (3) “deviation” from the assigned arm (i.e., 5th vaccine dose for 4th-dose-exposed, 4th dose for 4th-dose-unexposed); (4) or non-COVID death. All vaccines administered were monovalent (non-Omicron adapted). We calculated the rate difference (RD) per 1000 person-years, and we calculated 95% confidence intervals for the rate differences using the bootstrap method.32 We calculated estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs using overlap PS–weighted Cox proportional hazards regression models while accounting non-COVID death as a competing risk using the Fine-Gray method.33 We tested the proportional hazards assumption using the Kolmogorov-type supremum test.34 We produced cumulative incidence curves using cumulative incidence functions with overlap PS weighting. We also planned secondary subgroup analyses to assess the effectiveness among specified subgroups, including those defined by age, sex, comorbidity burden (by Charlson Comorbidity Index), type of DMARD, presence of ILD, type of rheumatic disease, history of prior SARS-CoV-2 infection, and interval between the 3rd dose and the index date. A two-sided p-value of <0·05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analysis was performed in SAS version 9.4 and R version 4.2.1.

This study was approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board. The funding agencies had no role in data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing of the manuscript or the decision to submit.

## Results

We included a total of 4305 unique patients with SARDs using DMARDs who received at least 3 mRNA vaccines and were eligible for a 4th dose during the study period. Of this group, 3126 received a 4th dose and 1179 had not yet received a 4th dose prior to 11/Jun/2022. After emulation of the time-sequential weekly trials as described in Figure S2, there were a total of 3126 participants who received a 4th vaccine and 38519 emulated participants who had not yet received a 4th dose. Median follow-up time was 135 d (112, 154) among patients receiving a 4th dose and 65 d (30, 156) among patients receiving no 4th dose yet. The proportion of censored subjects and reasons for censoring are reported in Table S4. After overlap PS weighting, both groups included N=2563 individuals; the interval from the 3rd dose to the index date was 177 d (161, 199) among patients receiving a 4th dose and 181 d (159, 209) among patients not yet receiving a 4th dose. Baseline covariates before and after PS overlap weighting are shown in Table 1. After overlap weighting, the mean age in each group was 67 years (SD 12 (4th dose), 4 (no 4th dose yet)), 73% (N=1863/2563) were female, 88% (N=2242/2563) were White, and the most common rheumatic disease was rheumatoid arthritis (54%, (N=1392/2563)) in each group (standardized mean difference <0.0001 for each covariate). Among patients identifying as being of non-White race, 4% (N=96/2563 in the 4th dose and N=106/2563 in the non-4th dose group) identified as Black or African American, 3% (N=80/2563 in the 4th dose and N=79/2563 in the non-4th dose group) identified as Asian, 2 to 3% (N=61/2563 in the 4th dose and N=65/2563 in the non-4th dose group) identified as other, 1% (N=21/2563 in the 4th dose and 18/2563 in the non-4th dose group) identified as being of two or more races, and 2% (N=62/2563 in the 4th dose and N=52/2563 in the non-4th dose group) had unknown race in the EHR. The most common DMARDs were csDMARDs (58%, N=1489/2563 in both groups) and bDMARDs (39%, N=1007/2563 in both groups). Between the 3rd vaccine dose and the index date, 1·8% (N=46/2563 in both groups) experienced a SARS-CoV-2 infection.

For the primary outcome, the incidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection was lower in the 4th dose group than those who had not yet received a 4th dose (incidence of 189 vs 296 per 1000 person-years; Table 2), with a rate difference between the two groups of −107 (95% CI: −162, −53) per 1000 person-years. In the primary analysis, receiving a 4th mRNA vaccine dose was associated with a 41% lower risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection than not yet receiving a 4th dose (Figure 1A, HR 0·59, 95% CI: 0·47, 0·74).

For the secondary outcome, the incidence rate of severe SARS-CoV-2 infection was 4·4 vs 11·3 per 1,000 person-years in the 4th dose cohort compared with those who had not yet received a 4th dose. The rate difference for severe SARS-CoV-2 infection was −6·9 (95% CI: −14, 0·24) with a hazard ratio of 0·35 (95% CI: 0·14, 0·85; Figure 1B).

We performed several pre-specified subgroup analyses (Table 3). As in the overall cohort, the median follow-up time in 4th-dose-exposed participants within these subgroups ranged from 118 to 149 days, and the median follow-up time in 4th-dose-unexposed participants ranged from 33 to 108 days (Table 3). The effectiveness of the 4th dose on the risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection did not vary significantly according to age or sex. The magnitude and direction of effect were similar among patients with Charlson Comorbidity Index scores of 0–1, 2–4, and 5+. Patients who had more recently (within 90–180 days) completed their 3-dose primary vaccine series had greater benefit from a 4th dose (HR 0·16; 95% CI: 0·10, 0·26) compared to those whose primary series was completed more than 6 months prior to their index date (HR 0·63; 95% CI: 0·46, 0·86). In the small subgroup of patients with a history of SARS-CoV-2 infection between the 3rd dose and the index date, there were few primary events and a wide confidence interval for the effect of a 4th dose (HR 0·44; 95% CI: 0·03, 5·68). Among those with no prior history of a SARS-CoV-2 infection, receiving a 4th dose of vaccine reduced the risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection (HR 0·59; 95% CI: 0·47, 0·74).

The effectiveness of a 4th mRNA vaccine dose was associated with a lower risk of the primary outcome similarly among most subgroups of DMARD users, including patients using bDMARDs (HR 0·64, 95% CI: 0·48, 0·88), csDMARDs (HR 0·58, 95% CI: 0·43, 0·77), oral glucocorticoids (HR 0·57, 95% CI: 0·32, 1·00), and tsDMARD users (HR 0·63, 95% CI: 0·19, 1·90). Among the small subgroup of rituximab users, we could not confirm a similar direction or magnitude of effect (HR 1·37, 95% CI: 0·32, 5·86).

## Discussion

In this emulated target trial, we found that a 4th dose of SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine was associated with significantly lower risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19-related hospitalization or death compared to not yet receiving a 4th dose among patients with SARDs using DMARDs. The effectiveness of a 4th dose was consistent across multiple subgroups stratified by age, sex, comorbidity burden, and DMARD subgroup. However, we could not confirm effectiveness among patients using rituximab and those with previous SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Our results support the current recommendation for booster vaccination in patients with SARDs using DMARDs.35 Despite these recommendations, vaccine uptake has been modest among immunocompromised patients, with only 41% of patients in a recent cohort having received the recommended 4 doses prior to August 2022.19 Further, survey studies have shown reduced uptake among patients with SARDs compared to patients in rheumatology clinics who do not have SARDs (i.e., those with osteoporosis or osteoarthritis).36 Factors affecting vaccine uptake among patients with rheumatic disease include concerns about side effects or disease flare, as well as uncertainty regarding vaccine efficacy.37 Our observations provide needed evidence regarding the effectiveness of booster vaccination in this vulnerable population and should help inform discussions with patients who remain concerned or uncertain about the potential benefits of boosters. Moreover, as efficacy of SARS-CoV-2 vaccinations wanes over time, the pandemic evolves and new variants emerge, our findings support recommendations from public health bodies for patients receiving DMARDs to remain up-to-date with current vaccine formulations, such as the XBB.1.5 monovalent vaccine that was recently recommended.35

We found a similar effect size to that reported in a recent study by Bieber et al, who conducted a retrospective analysis of 43,748 patients with SARDs in Israel and assessed the risk of COVID-19 infection and COVID-19 related hospitalization and death among patients who did versus did not yet receive a 4th mRNA vaccine dose.20 The authors reported a HR of 0·54 for the primary outcome of COVID-19 infection, HR of 0·36 for COVID-19 related hospitalization and 0·41 for COVID-related death, using propensity scores to adjust for imbalance between groups. Of note, due to privacy restrictions relating to the national health database, they were not able to confirm SARD diagnosis by medical record review and case identification was performed with International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes. Unlike our study, they did not perform time-stratified analyses that finely accounted for possible temporal trends related to vaccine recommendations/availability and novel SARS-CoV-2 variants; they were also unable to validate their SARD case-finding algorithm, included only patients receiving BNT162b2, and excluded patients with prior COVID-19 infection.

Our study expands upon these previous findings in several ways. We restricted our analysis to patients with SARDs using DMARDs, many of which have been associated with blunted responses to the original vaccine series. We were also able to validate the rules-based algorithm we used to identify cases, which had a PPV of 90%.5,38 Additionally, in contrast to previous analyses, we did not exclude patients with a prior history of COVID infection, which enhances generalizability: as of February 2022, approximately 60% of people in the United States were believed to have experienced a COVID-19 infection.39 Our subgroup analysis of patients with prior SARS-CoV-2 infections did not show a statistically significant protective effect of the 4th dose; this finding must be interpreted in the context of the small number of events in the subgroup but it may suggest that in SARD patients with hybrid immunity the marginal effect of a 4th dose on preventing any SARS-CoV-2 infection could be blunted. This possibility is supported by the findings of Bjørlykke et al, who noted a robust serologic response among SARD patients on DMARDs with hybrid immunity (3 vaccines plus a SARS-CoV-2 infection) that matched or exceeded that of patients with 4 vaccine doses but no infection.17 Further research is needed to develop recommendations regarding SARS-CoV-2 vaccination series in these patients, as well as to assess the optimal timing of booster dosing after a SARS-CoV-2 infection given the potential for a time-varying effect of infection on vaccine efficacy. Our current sample size limits our ability to analyze outcomes in these subgroups.

Our subgroup analyses did not confirm a protective effect of the 4th dose of mRNA vaccine among patients receiving B-cell depleting therapy. Although this subgroup analysis was limited by a smaller sample size, a blunted effect in rituximab users is biologically plausible as patients receiving rituximab are known to be at risk for particularly poor response to vaccination.40 Unfortunately, the current preventative armamentarium for B-cell depleted patients is severely limited: the US Food and Drug Administration formally revoked the emergency use authorization for tixagevimab/cilgavimab as pre-exposure prophylaxis in January, 2023 due to loss of neutralizing ability to circulating SARS-CoV-2 variants.41 Our data highlight the ongoing unmet need for preventative therapy to reduce the risk of COVID-19 related morbidity and mortality in patients on B-cell depleting therapy.

This study has several important strengths. Our use of a target trial design reduces the risk of confounding by prespecifying potential confounders and emulating a trial in which these variables are balanced between groups. The inclusion of time stratification is also an important strength of our analysis, as rates of infection have shown significant seasonal variation. Further, our cohort includes patients with diverse rheumatic diseases receiving multiple types of DMARD and our findings are therefore generalizable in rheumatologic practice.

Our findings are also subject to certain limitations. First, we were unable to verify whether patients were taking their prescribed immunomodulatory therapy, and whether they withheld any doses of DMARDs around the time of vaccination as per current recommendations. Since we used administrative data to identify immunomodulatory medication use before 3rd dose of vaccine, it is possible that patients may have discontinued the medication or temporarily interrupted medications around vaccine dose. Second, the transition from primary PCR to home antigen testing does raise the likelihood that infections occurred which were not captured in our health record, a possibility that is highlighted by the relatively low proportion of patients with recorded prior SARS-CoV-2 infections. However, if rates of unreported home antigen testing were different between those who did and did not yet receive a 4th dose, we would expect this to bias our findings in the opposite direction from that observed. That is, patients who received a 4th dose (and therefore may have greater healthcare exposure or greater health-consciousness) would be more likely to report their home positive tests to receive antiviral treatment. Our findings should be interpreted with the understanding that hazard ratios are generally limited by selection bias because the hazard in a given time period is assessed only in individuals who reach the time period in question free of the outcome of interest. Additionally, those who received a 4th dose had lower risk of severe COVID-19 in Cox models. While this was not statistically significant in the rate difference measure, the findings were overall similar. This may provide rationale for clinicians to recommend a 4th dose to potentially lower risk of severe COVID-19.

As this is an observational study, we were unable to control for unmeasured confounding and there may be measurement error in the covariates, such as smoking status, that were included in our models. Potential confounders include patient-level health consciousness and behaviors, including masking and avoidance of high risk exposures, which we were not able to assess. We were unable to determine the dose of vaccine (full dose versus “booster” dosing) as we did not have data regarding the specific dose received by each patient. However, we were able to account for mRNA vaccine types received. Our study was performed in a single health system, whereas vaccine efficacy is typically best assessed in larger multi-center studies. Although our health system includes multiple hospitals and health centers in both urban and rural communities, several of the subgroup analyses are limited by small sample size. The small size of these subgroups may predispose to sparse data bias.42 Finally, as the vaccines used in this study were monovalent, original type vaccines, future studies are needed to investigate updated vaccines and outcomes among patients with SARDs.

## Conclusion

In this emulated target trial, a fourth dose of COVID-19 mRNA vaccine was associated with a reduced risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection and severe COVID-19 among patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases using DMARDs during the Omicron era. Patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases should be encouraged to receive at least four doses of mRNA vaccines.
